opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way we think about it is that inference is where AI actually meets the real world. Training a model, fine-tuning it, evaluating it, all of that matters, but none of it creates value for an end user until the model is serving requests in production, with the latency, quality, and cost profile that a real product demands. So if you're building a platform for developers who want to ship AI applications, inference has to be the core you build everything else around.

When we started Fireworks, a lot of us came from running PyTorch at Meta, and we'd seen firsthand how hard it is to take a model from research into production at scale. The gap is enormous. You have to deal with GPU efficiency, batching, memory management, quantization, speculative decoding, routing across hardware, and on and on. Most application developers don't want to become experts in all of that. They want to focus on their product. So we invested very deeply in making the inference engine fast, reliable, and cost-efficient first, because if that layer isn't excellent, nothing you put on top of it really matters.

Once you have that foundation, the rest of the platform follows naturally. Developers start with an open model, they hit a quality ceiling for their specific use case, and then they want to customize: fine-tune on their own data, do reinforcement learning, build compound systems with multiple models and tools. But every one of those steps loops back into inference. Your fine-tuned model has to be served efficiently. Your evaluation runs are inference workloads. Even RL is extremely inference-heavy, since you're generating rollouts constantly. So inference isn't just the last step in the pipeline. It's the engine running underneath the whole development lifecycle.

That's why we describe it as the foundation. If you nail inference, you can build a tight loop where developers iterate on quality, latency, and cost together, and own their model and their data along the way. That end-to-end loop is really what we're trying to enable.

r001.rationale: The response says developers start with an open model and may customize it, but does not attribute Fireworks’ choice to build on open models rather than pretrain foundation models to the quality of available open models.

r002.rationale: It says reinforcement learning is inference-heavy because it involves constantly generating rollouts.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, thanks for having me, Sam. So the way I think about it is, when we started Fireworks, we actually spent a lot of time thinking about where the real pain was for developers who wanted to build with generative AI. And what we kept hearing, over and over, was that getting a model to run well in production was the hard part. Not experimenting with it, not getting a demo working. Actually shipping something that's fast enough, cheap enough, and reliable enough that you can put real users on it.

And inference is where all of that comes together. It's the point where the model actually meets the product. Every decision you make upstream, which model you pick, whether you fine-tune it, how you prompt it, what data you feed it, all of that only matters if it translates into something that works at serving time, at the latency and the cost your application can tolerate.

So for us, inference wasn't just one feature among many. It was the thing that had to be excellent first, because it's the foundation everything else sits on. If your inference stack is slow or expensive, then fine-tuning doesn't help you, because you can't afford to serve the model you tuned. Model customization doesn't help you, because you can't iterate fast enough to learn what's working. And so we started there, building the serving layer, optimizing kernels, doing the work on quantization and speculative decoding and so on, to get the latency and throughput to a place where developers could actually build on top of it.

Once you have that, something interesting happens. You start to see the whole loop. Developers want to take a model, run it on their traffic, look at what's going well and what isn't, collect that data, tune the model, and then put the improved version right back into serving. That's the flywheel. And you can't close that loop unless inference is at the center of it, because inference is both where the value is delivered and where the signal comes from.

That's really the thesis. A lot of the industry treats training as the center of gravity, and that makes sense for the frontier labs. But for the vast majority of developers and companies building products, the center of gravity is inference. It's the thing they interact with every single day, it's the thing that determines their unit economics, and it's the thing that determines whether their users have a good experience. So we built the platform outward from there.

r001.rationale: The response says Fireworks built its platform outward from inference, but does not attribute a choice to use open models instead of pretraining foundation models to the quality of available open models.

r002.rationale: The response describes inference as a source of product value and feedback for tuning, but does not explain that reinforcement fine-tuning relies on inference to generate training rollouts.

astra-6.text:
I think inference is where the model actually becomes part of an application. You can have a very capable model, but to build a useful product around it, you need to serve it with the right latency, reliability, and cost. And those requirements become especially important as you move from a prototype to production.

That’s why we see inference as the foundation. But developers don’t just need an endpoint. They need to figure out which model works for their use case, evaluate it on their data, and potentially customize it. Then they need to deploy it and learn from how it performs in the application.

Those steps are connected. A model that looks great in an offline evaluation may be too slow or too expensive for the experience you want to build. By building the platform around inference, we can bring those production constraints into the development process and help developers iterate toward an application that actually works for their users.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention open models, pretraining foundation models, or model quality as the reason for that choice.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss reinforcement fine-tuning or inference generating training rollouts.

sol-6.1.text:
Because inference is where the model actually becomes part of an application. Developers need to take a model, run it on their data, and see whether it delivers the quality, latency, and cost their use case requires. So we see inference as the foundation that the rest of the developer workflow builds on.

Once you have that foundation, you can help developers iterate: evaluate the model, customize it when needed, deploy it, and use what they learn from production to improve it. Those steps are closely connected. A customization is only useful if you can serve it efficiently and see an improvement in the application.

That’s why we start with inference and build the platform around it—to make that whole iteration loop easier for developers.

r001.rationale: The response describes inference as the foundation of Fireworks’ developer workflow, but does not attribute a choice to build on open models rather than pretrain foundation models, or cite the quality of available open models.

r002.rationale: The response discusses model customization and iteration but does not mention reinforcement fine-tuning or inference generating training rollouts.
